query: Consider noble metal–based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles containing more than five elements and targeted in a single-phase solid-solution state. Their crystal structure is difficult to control at fixed composition, while unsuccessful formation can involve phase separation, elemental segregation, uncontrolled particle morphology, and high thermal decomposition temperatures under synthesis regimes with rapid heating and cooling. What testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs formation and crystal-structure selection in this regime and why? Define a controlled intervention without specifying a technique, predict the observations relative to the initial single-phase baseline, identify the applicable compositional and processing boundaries, cite supporting evidence, and state a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In noble metal–based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles (e.g., composed of >5 elements such as Pt, Pd, Au, Ir, Rh) initially synthesized via rapid Joule heating to yield a disordered solid-solution state, an intermediate dwell at ~1100 K for a critical duration (approximately 5 minutes, with a tolerance of ±1 minute) followed by ultrafast cooling (~10^4 K/s) kinetically limits atomic mobility; this restricted diffusion promotes a thermodynamically favored yet kinetically trapped single-phase solid solution. Deviations from this dwell time (i.e., significantly longer or shorter durations) will lead to either the onset of phase separation, elemental segregation, or uncontrolled particle morphology.
generation.material_initial_state: Disordered solid-solution high-entropy alloy nanoparticles produced by an ultrafast (tens of milliseconds) Joule-heating process at ~1100 K.
generation.intervention: Introduce a controlled intermediate reheating step at ~1100 K with a dwell time targeted at approximately 5 minutes (testable variations in the range 4–6 minutes) before executing a rapid quench.
generation.conditions: The nanoparticles are maintained under an inert or reductive atmosphere to avoid oxidation, with precise thermal control; the cooling rate is maintained around 10^4 K/s. The intervention should be performed on compositions with over five noble metal components targeted in near equimolar ratios.
generation.structural_mediator: Atomic-scale mixing and short-range order that manifests as the formation of a uniform crystal structure (e.g., ordered intermetallic-like configuration within a single-phase solid solution) without significant particle growth, segregation, or phase separation.
generation.mechanism: Limited atomic mobility during the 5-minute reheating phase enables the system to undergo a disorder-to-order phase transition where thermodynamic driving forces lower the Gibbs free energy of the ordered state, while the rapid cooling kinetically traps this configuration. If the dwell time is too short, insufficient rearrangement prevents complete ordering; if too long, excessive mobility permits elemental segregation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Nanoparticles subjected to the optimal dwell time will exhibit a uniform, single-phase solid solution (confirmed by narrow diffraction peaks and homogeneous elemental distribution in TEM/EDS), whereas samples processed with non-optimal dwell times will display signs of phase separation, elemental segregation, or uncontrolled particle coarsening relative to the baseline.
generation.baseline: Nanoparticles produced by rapid Joule-heating alone that initially form a disordered solid-solution state without an intermediate dwell.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies to noble metal systems with more than five elements in near equimolar ratios; the thermal conditions (reheating at ~1100 K for 4–6 minutes and cooling rates around 10^4 K/s) represent the processing boundaries. Outside these ranges, either insufficient atomic rearrangement or excessive diffusion may occur.
generation.uncertainty: The exact optimal dwell time and cooling rate may depend on the specific combination of noble metals and their inherent mixing enthalpies; furthermore, potential variations in precursor chemistry might influence the effectiveness of the kinetic trapping process.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of noble metal HEA nanoparticles under otherwise identical conditions while varying only the intermediate dwell time at ~1100 K (e.g., 3 min, 5 min, 7 min) and maintaining the same rapid cooling rate. Analyze the crystallographic phase, particle morphology, and elemental distribution for each set.
measurements: X-ray diffraction (XRD) to assess single-phase vs. multiphase structures
High-resolution TEM with EDS mapping to evaluate particle size uniformity and elemental segregation
Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) to monitor phase transition signatures
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If extending or reducing the dwell time does not result in statistically significant deviations (e.g., emergence of secondary phases, increased segregation, or altered particle morphology) when compared to the baseline 5-minute dwell condition, then the hypothesis that a narrowly defined dwell time is critical for kinetically trapping the single-phase state would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractHigh entropy alloys (HEAs) are an important new material class with significant application potential in catalysis and electrocatalysis. The entropy-driven formation of HEA materials requires high temperatures and controlled cooling rates. However, catalysts in general also require highly dispersed materials, i.e., nanoparticles. Only then a favorable utilization of the expensive raw materials can be achieved. Several recently reported HEA nanoparticle synthesis strategies, therefore, avoid the high-temperature regime to prevent particle growth. In our work, we investigate a system of five noble metal single-source precursors with superior catalytic activity for the oxygen reduction reaction. Combining in situ X-ray powder diffraction with multi-edge X-ray absorption spectroscopy, we address the fundamental question of how single-phase HEA nanoparticles can form at low temperatures. It is demonstrated that the formation of HEA nanoparticles is governed by stochastic principles and the inhibition of precursor mobility during the formation process favors the formation of a single phase. cited_evidence.text: The combined data analyses from XRD and XAS evidence clearly that the elements in the five-metal precursor reduce stepwise. However, a single-phase alloy forms nonetheless. This behavior contrasts with the bimetallic case, suggesting that the rules governing phase formation differ for the systems containing two or five elements: Single-phase alloy formation occurs more readily if more elements are present, as systems that are immiscible on the bimetallic level can be driven to mix by introducing more elements. As the resulting phases of the binary particles cannot readily be explained by their thermodynamic stability, we devised a kinetic model to rationalize the experimental results based on the restrictions imposed by the synthesis. When comparing five-element and two-element mixtures, the concentration of individual atom types is reduced the more elements are present. This will make it increasingly difficult for elements with strong preferences of ordering to form an intermetallic structure or for elements that repulse each other to segregate, simply because they are more dilute. To address the above challenge, we propose an ultrafast (<100 ms), one-step method for the continuous synthesis of HEA NPs directly from a mixture of pure elemental metal powders by using a thermal plasma jet. Thermal plasma jets are partially ionized gases with high temperature (>8000 K) and high speed. They are capable of rapid heating of feedstock to produce an atomically mixed multi-component vapor, and also rapid cooling of the vapor at an ultrahigh cooling rate of 105 − 106 K s−1 to form solid-solution particles. Feedstock can be injected continuously, thus this technology is well suited for scalable synthesis of HEA NPs. Despite this unique potential, thermal plasma jets have only been used for the processing of bulk HEAs or spheroidization of pre-alloyed HEA powders. The main challenge would be the existence of a large nucleation temperature gap among different metal vapors; upon plasma jet cooling, the element with the lowest saturation vapor pressure reaches the supersaturated state first and segregates.

In this work, we demonstrate the synthesis of nanoscale MPEIs (4 to 5 nm) that contain up to eight different elements without particle growth or phase separation via a unique multi-elemental disorder-to-order (HEA to MPEI) phase transition strategy (Fig. 1A). Specifically, we first rapidly Joule-heated metal salt precursors on the carbon substrate [x-ray diffraction (XRD) and scanning electron microscopy characterization in fig. S2] at ~1100 K for 55 ms to produce disordered solid-solution HEA nanoparticles as the starting material (). We then use the precise heating control made possible by this Joule-heating approach (in which the reaction temperature is controlled by an electric current) to reheat the HEA nanoparticles for just 5 min at ~1100 K to promote atomic rearrangement to a more thermodynamically stable MPEI configuration (i.e., a disorder-to-order transition), followed by rapid cooling to lock the final ordered structure in place. The resulting MPEI nanoparticles feature an intermetallic structure that has two sublattices (A1B1) (fig. S3a). S5) the materials with precise control of the temperature and heating/cooling rates by tuning the power applied to the substrate (fig. S6). The temperature profile and structural evolution of nanoparticles over time are illustrated in Fig. 2A. We first synthesize solid-solution (HEA) nanoparticles () by heating the metal precursors for tens of milliseconds at ~1100 K. This is a critical step for mixing the different elements without phase separation. A disorder-to-order phase transition is then achieved by rapidly reheating the materials to ~1100 K for an additional ~5 min—a limited amount of time that is sufficient to complete the desired transition from the disordered HEA structure to the ordered, single-phase MPEI configuration while simultaneously avoiding nanoparticle growth/agglomeration. Last, the single-phase MPEI structure and small particle size (~5 nm) is preserved by rapidly cooling the materials (~104 K/s).

papers.title: Multi‐principal elemental intermetallic nanoparticles synthesized via a disorder‐to‐order transition.
papers.system: Noble metal–based HEA nanoparticles (e.g., octonary Pt0.8Pd0.1Au0.1–FeCoNiCuSn system) targeted toward ordered intermetallic (L10) structures.
papers.approach: Starting with rapid Joule-heating to form disordered solid-solution HEA nanoparticles followed by a short (~5 min) reheating step at ~1100 K and rapid quenching to induce a disorder-to‐order phase transition.
papers.findings: Successful conversion of disordered HEA to ordered MPEI nanoparticles with uniform ~4–5 nm sizes, preventing particle growth, agglomeration, and phase separation; achieved even when constituent elements are thermodynamically immiscible under slow-heating regimes.
papers.mechanism: Limited atomic mobility in the solid precursor combined with a short heating duration favors a thermodynamically driven disorder-to‐order transition, locking in an intermetallic structure before kinetic processes (e.g., phase separation or segregation) can occur.

papers.title: Continuous synthesis of high-entropy alloy nanoparticles by in-flight alloying of elemental metals.
papers.system: High-entropy alloy nanoparticles (e.g., CrFeCoNiMo system), with discussion broadly applicable to multicomponent systems including noble metal alloys.
papers.approach: Utilizing an ultrafast (<100 ms) one‐step synthesis via a high‐temperature thermal plasma jet with controlled heating and ultrahigh cooling rates, employing reactor geometry and plasma gas selection to promote turbulent mixing.
papers.findings: Demonstrated synthesis of well-mixed HEA nanoparticles despite large differences in elemental saturation pressures; noted potential segregation when elements nucleate at different temperatures; revealed that plasma gas choice (hydrogen vs helium) affects the residence time in molten state and thus overall alloy homogeneity.
papers.mechanism: Rapid vaporization and near-simultaneous nucleation (co-nucleation) are enabled by turbulent mixing and fast cooling, which overcome the nucleation temperature gap among constituent metals. The dilution of partial pressures (Pi = Ptotal/N) due to multiple elements further aids in preventing pure-metal nucleation.

papers.title: The more the better: on the formation of single-phase high entropy alloy nanoparticles as catalysts for the oxygen reduction reaction.
papers.system: Noble metal‐based HEA nanoparticles composed of five noble metals (Pt, Ir, Rh, Os, Ru) targeting single-phase solid solutions.
papers.approach: Preparation via a single-source precursor that is thermally decomposed under controlled low-temperature conditions; accompanied by in situ characterization (XRD, XAS) and kinetic simulation of nanoparticle formation.
papers.findings: Observed that the formation of a single-phase HEA is more readily achieved when more different metals are present, attributed to a stochastic reduction in the free mobility of any one element, which prevents preferential atomic ordering or segregation observed in binary systems.
papers.mechanism: The “stochastic mixing” hypothesis: as the number of elements increases, the dilute concentration of any individual atom severely limits its ability to form ordered or segregated clusters, thus favoring a random, single-phase solid solution even under kinetically restricted conditions.

papers.title: Kinetically Limited Phase Formation of Pt‐Ir Based Compositionally Complex Thin Films.
papers.system: Noble metal-based thin films (Pt-Ir, with variations by substituting Ag vs Pd) which are analogous in kinetic constraints to nanoparticle systems.
papers.approach: Vapor-phase deposition with controlled conditions; systematic substitution study comparing Ag and Pd to evaluate effects on diffusion barriers and phase formation.
papers.findings: Revealed that substituting Pd with Ag lowers the activation energy barrier for surface diffusion by about 35%, resulting in increased atomic mobility and thus promoting phase separation and dual-phase formation instead of a single metastable phase.
papers.mechanism: Kinetic control via surface diffusion: higher activation energy barriers limit atomic mobility and favor kinetically trapped single-phase formation, whereas lower barriers permit sufficient diffusion for the formation of segregated or multiple phases despite similar thermodynamic driving forces.

papers.title: A PtPdCoCuNi high-entropy alloy nanocatalyst for the hydrogenation of nitrobenzene.
papers.system: Noble metal-containing HEA nanoparticles (PtPdCoCuNi) supported on SiO2.
papers.approach: Synthesis of colloidal nanoparticles followed by thorough morphological and structural characterization (TEM, HRTEM, XRD, EDS mapping, XPS) to confirm uniform elemental distribution and fcc crystal structure maintained after reduction.
papers.findings: Produced uniform, ~7 nm diameter nanoparticles with an atomically homogenous distribution of five metals and an fcc crystal structure, consistent with theoretical thermodynamic parameters for single-phase HEAs.
papers.mechanism: A balanced interplay between thermodynamics (appropriate mixing entropy and enthalpy) and rapid kinetic quenching stabilizes the single-phase solid solution; controlled conversion conditions prevent phase segregation even in a multicomponent system.

established: Rapid heating and ultrafast cooling can kinetically trap metastable single-phase structures in high-entropy alloy nanoparticles.
Increasing the number of constituent elements dilutes individual atomic ordering tendencies, favoring random, homogeneous mixing.
Atomic mobility during synthesis, controlled by heating duration and cooling rate, is crucial for preventing phase separation and elemental segregation.
Reactor conditions (e.g., turbulence, plasma gas type, reactor geometry) significantly impact particle nucleation and growth dynamics.

approaches_tried.approach: Joule-heating based disorder-to-order transition with controlled short heating pulses followed by rapid quenching.
approaches_tried.outcome: Successful formation of ultrafine, ordered intermetallic nanoparticles (MPEIs) while avoiding agglomeration and phase separation.

approaches_tried.approach: Thermal plasma jet synthesis with in-flight alloying and engineered turbulence (using different plasma gases).
approaches_tried.outcome: Enhanced mixing and control over nucleation despite differences in individual elemental vapor pressures, though segregation may occur if cooling is not optimal.

approaches_tried.approach: Single-source precursor decomposition at moderate temperatures to limit precursor mobility.
approaches_tried.outcome: Formation of single-phase nanoparticles attributed to inhibition of atomic diffusion, as supported by kinetic modeling.

approaches_tried.approach: Vapor deposition with controlled surface diffusion, analyzing the effect of substituting elements (Ag vs Pd).
approaches_tried.outcome: Demonstrated sensitivity of phase formation to diffusion kinetics; lower diffusion barriers resulted in phase separation rather than single-phase formation.

mechanisms: Disorder-to-order phase transition driven by thermodynamic stabilization when limited atomic mobility is imposed.
Stochastic mixing enhanced by increasing the number of elements, leading to a suppression of ordered segregation.
Kinetic limitation of atomic diffusion; higher activation energy barriers can trap metastable single-phase states.
Co-nucleation in rapid, turbulent plasma environments can overcome differences in individual elemental saturation vapor pressures.
disagreements: Some studies emphasize thermodynamic driving forces (e.g., disorder-to-order transitions) while others point to kinetic limitations (e.g., surface diffusion barriers) as the dominant factor in phase selection.
The relative importance of precursor mobility versus vapor-phase mixing is debated between solid-state (precursor-based) and vapor-phase (plasma jet) synthesis methods.
open_questions: What are the precise quantitative limits of heating and cooling rates that consistently yield a single-phase solid solution in noble metal–based HEA nanoparticles?
How do variations in elemental composition (especially among noble metals) interact with kinetic barriers to influence phase segregation or ordering?
Can reactor geometry and plasma gas conditions be synergistically optimized to fully suppress unwanted phase separation in direct vapor synthesis methods?
What are the roles of potential ligand or precursor chemical effects on restricting atomic mobility during nanoparticle formation?
opportunities: Investigate a controlled intervention by finely tuning the heating duration and cooling rate (e.g., varying the reheating time around 5 min and adjusting quenching speed) during the disorder-to-order transition to test the influence on crystal structure selection.

Explore a combined approach that integrates the benefits of controlled Joule heating (for limited atomic mobility) with optimized plasma conditions (for enhanced elemental mixing) to expand the compositional space of noble metal-based HEA nanoparticles.

Design experiments to systematically vary the number of noble metal components while monitoring phase evolution; this would test the 'stochastic mixing' hypothesis and pinpoint compositional boundaries for single-phase formation.

Implement a controlled variation in surface diffusion activation energy (via targeted elemental substitution, e.g., tuning Ag vs Pd content) as a way to delineate kinetic versus thermodynamic contributions; an observation of phase separation when diffusion barriers drop below a threshold would falsify the hypothesis that kinetic confinement solely governs single-phase formation.

directions.direction: Increase the number of constituent elements to enhance stochastic mixing.
directions.assessment: By further diluting the concentration of any one species, stochastic mixing should prevent the onset of local ordering or phase segregation. This approach directly targets the underlying hypothesis that multi‐element dilution limits preferential clustering, as shown in studies (e.g., PMC10621632::web::000::abstract, PMC10621632::web::022::simulated_particle_formation_and_influen). However, compositional boundaries must be carefully defined to avoid overwhelming the system with excessive mixing enthalpy variations.

directions.direction: Fine-tune the thermal history by adjusting the intermediate dwell time and cooling rate.
directions.assessment: Controlling the dwell time at a fixed high temperature (e.g., ~1100 K) ensures limited atomic mobility that is sufficient for a disorder-to-order transition without triggering phase segregation. This mechanistic intervention directly addresses the kinetic limitations that lock in the single-phase solid solution, as evidenced by rapid Joule-heating studies (PMC8797181::web::003::introduction, PMC8797181::web::005::results) and kinetic models (PMC10621632::web::022::simulated_particle_formation_and_influen). It is feasible and allows systematic variation around the critical time constants.

directions.direction: Modulate the effective surface diffusion by substituting elements with different activation energy barriers (e.g., swapping Pd with Ag).
directions.assessment: Since studies comparing systems with Pd versus Ag illustrate that lower activation energy barriers lead to increased atomic mobility and unwanted phase separation (PMC7288289::web::004::1_introduction, PMC7288289::web::017::3_results_and_discussion), a deliberate substitution can be used to assess the sensitivity of phase selection to kinetic constraints. This approach directly tests whether kinetic confinement is the controlling factor for maintaining single-phase HEA nanoparticles.

directions.direction: Optimize reactor flow conditions (e.g., turbulence and plasma gas choice) to control the nucleation and mixing during vapor-phase synthesis.
directions.assessment: Adjusting reactor geometry and plasma gas parameters can affect both the nucleation temperature gap and the residence time in the molten state, impacting elemental mixing (PMC10873330::web::003::introduction, PMC10873330::web::024::effect_of_plasma_gases). While this method addresses phase control in the vapor‐phase approach, it is less directly related to the kinetic confinement observed in solid precursor studies and may introduce additional variables that obscure the mechanistic understanding.

directions.direction: Perform in-situ structural and spectroscopic characterization during synthesis to monitor real-time atomic rearrangements.
directions.assessment: By employing in-situ XRD and XAS during the heat treatment stage, one can directly observe the disorder-to-order transition and identify the time–temperature regimes that favor single-phase formation. This method would yield highly informative insights about the dynamical processes, although it requires complex instrumentation and may be less straightforward to implement during high-throughput nanoparticle synthesis.

choice.direction: Fine-tune the thermal history by adjusting the intermediate dwell time and cooling rate.
choice.why: Because a controlled thermal-profile intervention directly tests the hypothesis that limited atomic mobility at a critical temperature and time window is essential for locking in the single-phase solid-solution state. Evidence from Joule-heating based disorder-to-order transitions (PMC8797181::web::003::introduction, PMC8797181::web::005::results) and kinetic simulations (PMC10621632::web::022::simulated_particle_formation_and_influen) supports this approach as both mechanistically direct and experimentally feasible.
